name: Gevrey-Chambertin
style: Full-bodied, firm tannins, dark fruit (blackcurrant, plum), earthy. The most powerful village of the Côte de Nuits. Ages 10–20 years.
agingRules: Minimum 18 months in oak for village-level reds.
facts: The largest appellation in Côte de Nuits by area
Contains 9 Grands Crus, more than any other Burgundy village
Chambertin was Napoleon's favorite wine

name: Chambolle-Musigny
style: The most delicate and floral village of the Côte de Nuits. Violets, rose petal, red fruit. Silky texture, fine tannins. The 'feminine' counterpart to Gevrey.
facts: Home to the legendary Grand Cru Musigny
Les Amoureuses Premier Cru fetches prices rivaling many Grands Crus
The village name combines 'Chambolle' and the Musigny vineyard

name: Meursault
style: Rich, nutty, buttery white Burgundy. Toasted hazelnut, white peach, lanolin, and a mineral finish. The most important white wine village of the Côte de Beaune.
agingRules: Minimum 12 months in oak for whites.
facts: No Grand Crus, but Premiers Crus like Perrières and Charmes rival Grand Cru quality
The Paulée de Meursault is one of Burgundy's great annual wine festivals
Also produces a small amount of red under the Meursault AOC

name: Chablis
style: Lean, crisp, steely. Oyster shell, green apple, citrus, and flinty minerality. The antithesis of oaky Chardonnay. Often unoaked or aged in old oak.
agingRules: Typically aged in stainless steel; some producers use old oak.
facts: Grown on Kimmeridgian limestone with fossilized oyster shells — unique in the world
Four quality levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru, Grand Cru
Geographically isolated ~80km northwest of the Côte d'Or

name: Chablis
style: Lean, crisp, steely. Oyster shell, green apple, citrus, and flinty minerality. The antithesis of oaky Chardonnay. Often unoaked or aged in old oak.
agingRules: Typically aged in stainless steel; some producers use old oak.
facts: Grown on Kimmeridgian limestone with fossilized oyster shells
Four quality levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru, Grand Cru
7 Grands Crus all situated on a single southeast-facing slope north of the town

name: Marsannay
style: The only Côte de Nuits village that produces all three colours. The rosé is legendary — dry, mineral, strawberry-scented. Reds are lighter and earlier-drinking than its southern neighbours.
facts: The only Côte de Nuits AOC permitted to make rosé
Historically the northern gateway to the Côte de Nuits, just south of Dijon
Gained village AOC status only in 1987

name: Morey-Saint-Denis
style: Often overlooked between the famous Gevrey and Chambolle. Dark, structured, meaty reds with great aging potential. A hidden gem of the Côte de Nuits.
facts: Contains 5 Grands Crus: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos des Lambrays, Clos de Tart, and part of Bonnes-Mares
Sandwiched between Gevrey-Chambertin and Chambolle-Musigny
Clos de Tart is a monopole (single-owner Grand Cru) owned by Artémis Domaines

name: Vougeot
style: Dominated by Clos de Vougeot, a 50ha Grand Cru owned by over 80 producers. Quality varies enormously by producer. The best examples are perfumed, rich, and complex.
facts: Clos de Vougeot is the largest Grand Cru in the Côte de Nuits at ~50 hectares
The château at its centre is now the headquarters of the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin
Over 80 different producers own parcels within Clos de Vougeot — quality varies dramatically

name: Vosne-Romanée
style: The most prestigious village in all of Burgundy. Silky, velvety, hauntingly complex. Spice, dark fruit, forest floor, and a perfumed length that can last for decades.
facts: Home to the world's most expensive wine: Romanée-Conti Grand Cru (~1.8 hectares, ~5,000 bottles per year)
Contains 6 Grands Crus: Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant, Grands-Echézeaux, Echézeaux
Even the village-level wines regularly outperform Grand Crus from lesser appellations

name: Nuits-Saint-Georges
style: Structured, earthy, and firm — the most 'masculine' of the Côte de Nuits villages. Dark fruit, game, and truffles. Requires patience; opens up beautifully after 8–15 years.
facts: No Grand Crus, but boasts 41 Premiers Crus — more than any other Burgundy village
The commercial capital of the Côte de Nuits — home to many négociants
The town added 'Saint-Georges' (its best Premier Cru) to its name in 1892 for marketing purposes

name: Aloxe-Corton
style: Produces the only red Grand Cru of the Côte de Beaune: Corton. Firm, structured reds that need time. The white Corton-Charlemagne is a majestic, mineral Chardonnay.
agingRules: Grand Cru minimum 18 months in oak; village minimum 12 months.
facts: Corton is the only red Grand Cru in the Côte de Beaune
Corton-Charlemagne — named after Charlemagne who owned vines here in the 8th century — is one of Burgundy's greatest whites
The Corton hill is shared between Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny, and Pernand-Vergelesses

name: Beaune
style: Fragrant, medium-bodied, elegant reds. Supple and approachable earlier than Pommard. The Premiers Crus (Grèves, Clos des Mouches) can be outstanding.
facts: The wine capital of Burgundy — home to many major négociant houses
No Grand Crus, but 42 Premiers Crus covering most of the appellation
The Hospices de Beaune charity auction, held every November, is the world's greatest wine auction

name: Pommard
style: The most full-bodied and tannic red of the Côte de Beaune. Dark fruit, game, earthy. Requires 10+ years to soften. Les Rugiens and Les Epenots are the top Premiers Crus.
facts: No Grand Crus but often called the 'Gevrey-Chambertin of the Côte de Beaune' for its power
Only red wine is produced here — no white Pommard AOC exists
The commune is entirely enclosed by walls — all 340 hectares are Premier Cru or village level

name: Puligny-Montrachet
style: The pinnacle of white Burgundy. Tense, mineral, complex. Almonds, white flowers, citrus, and a stony finish. Grand Crus (Montrachet, Chevalier) are among the greatest wines on earth.
agingRules: Minimum 12 months in oak; Grand Crus often 18+ months.
facts: Shares the Grand Cru Montrachet with neighbouring Chassagne-Montrachet
Grand Crus: Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet (partial), Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet
Alexandre Dumas said Montrachet should be drunk 'kneeling, with head bowed'

name: Chassagne-Montrachet
style: Whites are richer and broader than Puligny — more golden and nutty. Reds are often underrated, producing earthy, medium-bodied Pinot Noir at fair prices.
facts: Shares Grand Crus Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet with Puligny-Montrachet
Unlike Puligny, makes a significant amount of red wine (about 40% of production)
Often better value than Puligny at village level for comparable quality

name: Santenay
style: Earthy, rustic, reliable reds at the southern tip of the Côte de Beaune. Good value. Les Gravières and La Comme are the standout Premiers Crus.
facts: The southernmost village of the Côte de Beaune proper
A spa town — the mineral springs have attracted visitors since Roman times
Often overlooked, offering honest village-level Burgundy at approachable prices

name: Mercurey
style: The most serious red appellation of the Côte Chalonnaise. Firm, structured, earthy. Dark cherry, hints of smoke. Good aging potential for the price.
facts: The largest and most important appellation of the Côte Chalonnaise
32 Premiers Crus — the most of any Chalonnaise village
Named after the Roman god Mercury, reflecting the area's ancient wine-trading history

name: Givry
style: Lighter and more elegant than Mercurey. Cherry, raspberry, a touch of spice. Approachable young but rewards some cellaring. White Givry is floral and fresh.
facts: Reportedly the favourite wine of King Henri IV of France
About 85% of production is red wine
Located on the western bank of the Saône plain

name: Rully
style: Best known for whites and Crémant de Bourgogne. Light, floral Chardonnay with good freshness. Reds are light and perfumed. Excellent entry-level Burgundy.
facts: One of the main production centres for Crémant de Bourgogne (Burgundy sparkling wine)
About 60% of production is white wine — unusual for the Chalonnaise
23 Premiers Crus offering excellent value

name: Pouilly-Fuissé
style: The flagship of the Mâconnais. Richer and more golden than Chablis. Stone fruit, white flower, subtle oak. Can age well — 5 to 10 years for top examples.
agingRules: Often aged in oak barrels; some producers use new oak.
facts: Premiers Crus status was officially granted in 2020 — a major step up for the appellation
The vineyards are overshadowed by the dramatic Rock of Solutré and Rock of Vergisson
Despite its reputation, many examples offer fair value versus Côte de Beaune whites

name: Mâcon
style: Accessible, approachable, everyday Burgundy. Fresh white fruit, light body, clean finish. Best drunk young and fresh. The entry point to white Burgundy.
agingRules: Typically unoaked or lightly oaked; drink within 3–4 years.
facts: Mâcon-Villages (or Mâcon + village name) indicates superior quality from specific villages
The Mâconnais is the largest sub-region of Burgundy by area
About 80% of production is white wine (Chardonnay)

name: Saint-Véran
style: Fresh, fruity, unoaked Chardonnay. Pear, white flowers, a touch of almond. Rounder and fuller than Mâcon, leaner than Pouilly-Fuissé. Excellent value.
agingRules: Usually unoaked or old oak; drink within 4–5 years.
facts: Surrounds Pouilly-Fuissé on three sides — often compared favourably at a lower price
The appellation was created in 1971 as an alternative to Beaujolais Blanc
Includes villages as far south as Saint-Amour, bordering Beaujolais

name: Chambertin
style: The 'King of Burgundy.' Massive structure, black fruit, iron, earth, and extraordinary length. Demands 15–25 years to fully open. Among the most profound reds on earth.
agingRules: Minimum 18 months in oak. Top producers use 50–100% new oak.
facts: Napoleon Bonaparte reportedly insisted on Chambertin at every meal and carried it on military campaigns
The name derives from 'Champ de Bertin' — the field of a medieval peasant named Bertin
Shares its southern border with Latricières and its northern border with Clos de Bèze

name: Chambertin-Clos de Bèze
style: More elegant and perfumed than Chambertin, with silkier tannins. Red and black fruit, violets, spice, great complexity. Can be sold as Chambertin but not vice versa.
facts: Originally planted by monks from the Abbey of Bèze in the 7th century — Burgundy's oldest documented vineyard
Uniquely, producers may label it as simply 'Chambertin' — giving them two Grand Cru options
Often considered the more elegant twin to Chambertin, though debate continues

name: Chapelle-Chambertin
style: The lightest of the Gevrey Grands Crus. Floral, red fruit, delicate. Approachable earlier than its neighbours but still benefits from 10–15 years of cellaring.
facts: Named after a chapel built by the monks of Bèze that once stood at the site
At 5.5 ha, it is one of the smaller Gevrey Grands Crus
Shares a border with Clos de Bèze to the north and Griotte to the south

name: Charmes-Chambertin
style: Plush, seductive, round. Rich dark cherry, chocolate, and spice. The most approachable of the Gevrey Grands Crus in youth, with softer tannins and early allure.
facts: The largest of the nine Gevrey Grands Crus at ~30 ha — the Mazoyères section may be sold as Charmes
The name may derive from 'chaume' (fallow land) rather than the French word for charm
Lower-lying parcels can produce wines of lesser concentration than the hillside plots

name: Griotte-Chambertin
style: The most exotic and spicy of the Gevrey Grands Crus. Wild cherry (griotte), kirsch, floral notes, and a touch of game. Rare and sought-after.
facts: Named after the griotte cherry — the dominant flavour of wines from this climat
At only 2.7 ha, production is tiny — fewer than 10,000 bottles per year in total
Drouhin is the dominant owner with ~1.5 ha of the 2.7 ha total

name: Latricières-Chambertin
style: Wild, earthy, and structured. Forest floor, dark fruit, iron mineral. Often tannic in youth — a brooding style that rewards 15+ years of patience.
facts: Situated directly south of Chambertin and shares its powerful, structured character
The name may derive from 'latrines' — the rocky, poor soil that was historically used for waste
Leroy's holding is considered among the finest — they farm biodynamically

name: Mazis-Chambertin
style: Powerful, firm, and long-lived. Dark fruit, iron, earthy. Tight in youth, it unfolds over 15–20 years into a wine of great complexity and depth.
facts: Divided into two lieu-dits: Mazis-Haut (higher, stonier, finer) and Mazis-Bas (lower, richer)
Borders Ruchottes to the north — one of the northernmost Gevrey Grands Crus
Hospices de Beaune owns a famous cuvée from Mazis-Chambertin

name: Mazoyères-Chambertin
style: Virtually identical in character to Charmes-Chambertin — plush, round, fruit-forward. Most producers choose to label it as Charmes-Chambertin, which is legally permitted.
facts: Producers may legally label their wine as Charmes-Chambertin — few use the Mazoyères name
Occupies the lower portion of the Charmes-Chambertin climat, closer to the road
The distinction from Charmes is largely academic — the wines are indistinguishable in style

name: Ruchottes-Chambertin
style: The most mineral and austere of the Gevrey Grands Crus. Stony, tight, and tense in youth. Exceptional precision and length after 15–20 years.
facts: The highest-elevation Grand Cru in Gevrey-Chambertin — thin, rocky soils
Rousseau's 'Clos des Ruchottes' is effectively a monopole of the best parcels
At 3.4 ha, total production rarely exceeds 12,000 bottles

name: Bonnes-Mares
style: The powerful Grand Cru of Chambolle-Musigny. Structured and rich, with dark fruit, earth, and animal notes — the antithesis of the village's delicate style. Ages 20+ years.
facts: Straddles two communes: 13.7 ha in Chambolle-Musigny and 1.5 ha in Morey-Saint-Denis
The two soil types (red clay and white limestone) produce noticeably different wines within the same GC
Roumier's Bonnes-Mares is one of the most sought-after wines in Burgundy

name: Musigny
style: The most feminine Grand Cru of Burgundy. Exquisite perfume — violets, rose, red berries — wrapped in the finest silky tannins. Hauntingly complex, ages 20–30 years.
agingRules: Minimum 18 months in oak. De Vogüé uses 100% new oak.
facts: De Vogüé owns 7 of the 10.8 hectares — the benchmark for this appellation
One of the few Grand Crus to produce a tiny amount of white wine (Musigny Blanc from de Vogüé)
The name 'Musigny' may derive from 'muscs' — musky or perfumed

name: Clos Saint-Denis
style: The most delicate and feminine of the Morey Grands Crus. Floral, red fruit, silky. Less powerful than Clos de la Roche but highly refined. Best after 12–18 years.
facts: Morey-Saint-Denis added this Grand Cru's name to its own in 1927 — giving the village its current name
The smallest of the four Morey Grands Crus at 6.6 ha
Named after the priory of Saint-Denis de Vergy that owned the vineyard in the Middle Ages

name: Clos de la Roche
style: The most powerful Grand Cru of Morey-Saint-Denis. Dense, structured, earthy, with dark fruit and truffle. A 'Chambertin-like' wine that demands 15–25 years.
facts: The largest Morey Grand Cru at 17 ha — Ponsot's Cuvée Vieilles Vignes is legendary
Rocky, stonier soils than the Chambolle Grands Crus — responsible for its structured character
Named after a rocky outcrop within the vineyard

name: Clos des Lambrays
style: Elegant, precise, and perfumed. Red fruit, floral notes, fine tannins. Lighter in body than Clos de la Roche, closer in style to the Chambolle Grands Crus.
facts: Effectively a monopole — Domaine des Lambrays owns virtually all 8.8 hectares
Acquired by LVMH (Moët Hennessy) in 2014 for a reported €101 million
Promoted to Grand Cru status only in 1981 — one of the last additions to the GC hierarchy

name: Clos de Tart
style: Structured, concentrated, and silky. Red and black cherry, spice, earthy depth. The walled monopole produces wines of great consistency and terroir expression.
agingRules: Minimum 18 months in oak. Winemaker Jacques Devauges uses 30–50% new oak.
facts: A perfect monopole — the entire 7.5 ha is owned by Artémis Domaines (François Pinault)
The vineyard has been a single holding since the 12th century — owned by Cistercian nuns from 1141
Sold for an estimated €200 million to Pinault in 2017 — the most expensive vineyard sale in history

name: Clos de Vougeot
style: Varies enormously by producer and parcel. Top parcels (upper slope) produce profound, structured, complex reds. Lower parcels can be rich but looser. Quality is entirely producer-dependent.
facts: With 80+ different owners, Clos de Vougeot is the ultimate proof that terroir alone doesn't guarantee quality
The walled vineyard (clos) was assembled by Cistercian monks from the Abbey of Cîteaux between 1150–1336
The Château within the clos is home to the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin — Burgundy's most famous wine brotherhood

name: Echezeaux
style: The 'approachable' Grand Cru of Flagey. Lighter and more supple than its neighbour Grands-Echézeaux. Perfumed, red fruit, spice. Ready earlier — 10 to 15 years.
facts: At nearly 38 ha, Echézeaux is one of the largest Burgundy Grand Crus — divided into 11 individual lieux-dits
The quality varies dramatically between the top parcels (near Grands-Echézeaux) and those near the road
DRC produces a celebrated Echézeaux that is a fraction of the price of their other Grand Crus

name: Grands-Echézeaux
style: More powerful and structured than Echézeaux. Dark fruit, spice, floral notes, great depth. A bridge between the elegance of Vosne and the power of Clos de Vougeot. Needs 15+ years.
facts: Despite the name, 'Grands-Echézeaux' is not a superior version of Echézeaux — it is a separate, distinct climat
Directly adjacent to Clos de Vougeot — the soils and exposures are very similar
DRC's version is considered the benchmark — one of the more 'accessible' DRC Grand Crus

name: La Grande Rue
style: Sandwiched between La Tâche and Romanée-Conti, sharing the silky elegance of its famous neighbours. Perfumed, precise, red fruit, mineral depth. Best after 15 years.
facts: A monopole — François Lamarche owns all 1.65 ha
Promoted to Grand Cru status in 1992 — it was previously Premier Cru
Literally runs between La Romanée-Conti and La Tâche, making it arguably the most uniquely-situated Grand Cru

name: La Romanée
style: Delicate, precise, and ethereal. Red fruit, rose petal, spice, and extraordinary mineral tension. Tiny production makes this one of Burgundy's rarest wines.
facts: At 0.85 ha, La Romanée is the smallest Grand Cru appellation in all of France
A monopole owned entirely by the Liger-Belair family since the 19th century
Fewer than 3,000 bottles are produced in a typical vintage

name: La Tâche
style: Haunting, exotic, and complex. Spice, dark cherry, violet, and a characteristic iron-mineral finish. More structured than Romanée-Conti but equally profound. Peaks at 20–30 years.
facts: A DRC monopole — one of the few wholly-owned Grand Crus in Vosne-Romanée
At 6 ha, it is larger than Romanée-Conti and DRC's most abundantly produced Grand Cru
Prices rival Romanée-Conti — typically $3,000–$8,000 per bottle at retail

name: Richebourg
style: The most opulent and voluptuous Grand Cru of Vosne. Rich, velvety, perfumed. Cassis, roses, spice, and a majestic, lingering finish. Ages magnificently over 20–30 years.
facts: At 8 ha, it is the largest of the six DRC Grand Cru monopoles and near-monopoles in Vosne
The name 'Richebourg' ('rich hill') reflects the clay-rich soils that give wines their lush character
Leroy's Richebourg is considered by many to rival DRC's version

name: Romanée-Conti
style: The greatest wine in the world, according to many. Incomprehensible complexity — spice, fruit, earth, exotic perfume, and a finish that lasts minutes. Requires 20–40 years.
agingRules: Minimum 18 months in oak. DRC uses 100% new oak.
facts: A DRC monopole — one of the rarest and most expensive wines on earth (~5,000–6,000 bottles per year)
A single bottle regularly fetches $15,000–$50,000+ at auction; the 1945 vintage sold for $558,000
The Prince of Conti purchased the vineyard in 1760 and lent it his name — it was nationalised during the Revolution but returned to private ownership

name: Romanée-Saint-Vivant
style: The most delicate and ethereal of the six Vosne Grands Crus. Lighter in colour, floral, with red fruit and extraordinary mineral precision. A feminine counterpoint to Richebourg.
facts: Originally owned by the abbey of Saint-Vivant de Vergy — one of the oldest monastic vineyards in Burgundy
DRC controls 5.3 of the 9.4 ha; the remainder is split among several small producers
Often described as 'the most Burgundian of all Burgundies' for its translucent, ethereal style

name: Corton
style: The only red Grand Cru of the Côte de Beaune. Powerful, structured, earthy, with dark fruit and a firm mineral backbone. Can be austere in youth; opens magnificently after 15–20 years.
facts: The Corton hill is shared by three communes: Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny, and Pernand-Vergelesses
Wines may be labelled 'Corton' or 'Corton + lieu-dit' (e.g. Corton Clos du Roi, Corton Les Bressandes)
The hill produces both red (Corton) and white (Corton-Charlemagne) Grand Crus — unique in Burgundy

name: Corton-Charlemagne
style: Majestic white Burgundy. Powerful, mineral, and long-lived. Toasted almond, citrus, white flowers, and a stony, almost electric finish. Rivalled only by Montrachet among Burgundy whites.
agingRules: Minimum 12 months in oak; top producers 18+ months.
facts: Charlemagne (742–814) owned vines on this hill and is said to have introduced white grapes
Covers the upper western and southern flanks of the Corton hill — the white wine zone
Bonneau du Martray, with 9.5 ha, is the largest single owner and the benchmark producer

name: Charlemagne
style: Essentially identical to Corton-Charlemagne in style — powerful, mineral, complex white Burgundy. Almost never seen on labels as producers overwhelmingly prefer the more prestigious 'Corton-Charlemagne' designation.
facts: The 'Charlemagne' appellation is almost never used — producers may label their wine as 'Corton-Charlemagne' instead
Covers the Pernand-Vergelesses portion of the Grand Cru hill
Named after Emperor Charlemagne, who supposedly kept vines here in the 8th century

name: Montrachet
style: The greatest dry white wine on earth. Extraordinary richness, minerality, and complexity. Honey, white flowers, hazelnut, and a finish of breathtaking length. Must be aged 10–20 years.
agingRules: Minimum 12 months in oak; typically 18+ months for Grand Cru.
facts: Alexandre Dumas decreed it should be drunk 'kneeling, with head bowed and in a spirit of devotion'
Straddles the boundary of Puligny-Montrachet (southern part) and Chassagne-Montrachet (northern part)
DRC acquired 0.67 ha in 2018 — the most recent major transaction for this appellation

name: Chevalier-Montrachet
style: Higher, lighter, and more mineral than Montrachet. Electric, tense, and precise — citrus, white flower, and a steely, almost saline finish. Less opulent but arguably more intellectual.
agingRules: Minimum 12 months in oak; typically 18 months.
facts: Sits directly above Montrachet on the slope — thinner, more limestone-rich soils produce a leaner, more austere style
Leflaive is the dominant owner with ~2 ha of the 7.5 ha total
Often more consistent than Montrachet across difficult vintages due to its better drainage

name: Bâtard-Montrachet
style: Richer and more opulent than Chevalier, but less so than Montrachet. Hazelnut, cream, stone fruit, and a broad, generous finish. The most accessible of the Montrachet Grands Crus.
agingRules: Minimum 12 months in oak; typically 18 months.
facts: Straddles Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet — the boundary runs through the middle
At 11.9 ha, it is the largest of the Montrachet Grands Crus
The name 'Bâtard' (bastard) may refer to an illegitimate son of a medieval lord who inherited these vines

name: Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet
style: Lighter and more floral than Bâtard-Montrachet. Fresh citrus, almond, and white flowers with a fine mineral thread. Approachable earlier, typically at its best 8–15 years.
facts: Lies entirely within Puligny-Montrachet — there is no Chassagne component
The whimsical name translates as 'Welcome to Bâtard-Montrachet'
At 3.7 ha, production is limited — often overshadowed by its larger neighbour Bâtard

name: Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet
style: Rich and creamy with ripe stone fruit and hazelnut. The most Chassagne-like of the Montrachet Grands Crus — broader and more textural than Chevalier. Drink at 8–15 years.
facts: The smallest of the Montrachet Grand Crus at 1.57 ha — and lies entirely in Chassagne-Montrachet
Fewer than 6,000 bottles are produced annually across all producers
The name 'Criots' derives from the local dialect word for stony, cried-out (exhausted) soil
